{{Short description|Plot for enzyme kinetics data}}
[[File:Direct-linear-plot.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|Idealized direct linear plot without experimental error. To avoid crowding and confusion, not all of the rates are indicated explicitly.]]
In biochemistry, the '''direct linear plot''' is a graphical method for [[enzyme kinetics]] data following the [[Michaelis–Menten equation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Eisenthal |first1=Robert |last2=Cornish-Bowden |first2=Athel |year=1974 |title=The direct linear plot: a new graphical procedure for estimating enzyme kinetic parameters |journal=Biochem. J. |volume=139 |pages=715–720 |doi=10.1042/bj1390715 |number=3|pmid=4854723 |pmc=1166335 }}</ref> In this plot, observations are not plotted as points, but as ''lines'' in parameter space with axes <math>K_\mathrm{m}</math> and <math>V</math>, such that each observation of a rate <math>v_i</math> at substrate concentration  <math>a_i</math> is represented by a straight line with intercept <math>-a_i</math> on the <math>K_\mathrm{m}</math> axis and <math>v_i</math> on the <math>V</math> axis. Ideally (in the absence of experimental error) the lines intersect at a unique point <math>(\hat{K}_\mathrm{m}, \hat{V})</math> whose coordinates provide the values of <math>\hat{K}_\mathrm{m}</math> and <math>\hat{V}</math>.

==Comparison with other plots of the Michaelis–Menten equation==
The best known plots of the Michaelis–Menten equation, including the [[double-reciprocal plot]] of <math>1/v</math> against <math>1/a</math>,<ref name = linew>{{Cite journal|last1=Lineweaver|first1=H.|last2=Burk|first2=D.|date=1934|doi =  10.1021/ja01318a036| title=The Determination of Enzyme Dissociation Constants |journal=J. Amer. Chem. Soc.|language=en|volume=56|issue=3|pages=658–666|bibcode=1934JAChS..56..658L }}</ref> the [[Hanes plot]] of <math>a/v</math> against <math>a</math>,<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1042/bj0261406 | journal = Biochem. J.  |pages = 1406–1421 | volume = 26 | number = 2 | author = Hanes, C.S. | title = Studies on plant amylases. I. The effect of starch concentration upon the velocity of hydrolysis by the amylase of germinated barley | year = 1932| pmid = 16744959 | pmc = 1261052 }}</ref> and the [[Eadie–Hofstee plot]]<ref>{{cite journal | journal = J. Biol. Chem. | volume = 146 | number = 1 | title = The inhibition of cholinesterase by physostigmine and prostigmine | author = Eadie, G. S. | pages = 85–93 |  year =1942| doi = 10.1016/S0021-9258(18)72452-6 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | journal=J. Biol. Chem. | title = Specificity of esterases |volume = 199 | number = 1 | year = 1953 | author=Hofstee, B. H. J. | pages = 357–364| doi = 10.1016/S0021-9258(18)44843-0 | doi-access = free }}</ref> of <math>v</math> against <math>v/a</math> are all plots in '''observation space''', with each observation represented by a point, and the parameters determined from the slope and intercepts of the lines that result. This is also the case for non-linear plots, such as that of <math>v</math> against <math>a</math>, often wrongly called a "Michaelis-Menten plot", and that of <math>v</math> against <math>\log a</math> used by Michaelis and Menten.<ref name="michaelis13">{{Cite journal| last1 = Michaelis|first1 = L.| last2 = Menten| first2  = M. L.| year = 1913| title = Die Kinetik der Invertinwirkung| journal = Biochem. Z.| volume = 49| pages = 333–369}}</ref> In contrast to all of these, the direct linear plot is a plot in '''[[parameter space]],''' with observations represented by lines rather than as points.

==Effect of experimental error==
[[File:Realistic direct linear plot with errors.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|In reality, the intersection points in a direct linear plot are subject to experimental error, which may be very large. To avoid overcrowding, only two of the six intersection points are explicitly labelled.]]
The case illustrated above is idealized, because it ignores the effect of [[experimental error]]. In practice, with <math>n</math> observations, instead of a unique point of intersection, there is a ''family'' of <math>n(n-1)/2</math> intersection points, with each one giving a separate estimate of <math>K_{\mathrm{m}_{ij}}</math> and <math>V_{ij}</math> for the lines drawn for the <math>i\,\mathrm{th}</math> and <math>j\,\mathrm{th}</math> observations.<ref name=stat>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1042/bj1390721 | journal = Biochem. J. | volume = 130 | number = 3 | pages = 721–730 |author1=Cornish-Bowden, A. |author2=Eisenthal, R. | title = Statistical considerations in estimation of enzyme kinetic parameters by the direct linear plot and other methods| year = 1974 | pmid = 4854389 | pmc = 1166336 }}</ref> Some of these, when the intersecting lines are almost parallel, will be subject to very large errors, so one must not take the means (weighted or not) as the estimates of <math>\hat{K}_\mathrm{m}</math> and <math>\hat{V}</math>. Instead one can take the [[median]]s of each set as estimates <math>K_\mathrm{m}^*</math> and <math>V^*</math>.

The great majority of intersection points should occur in the [[first quadrant]] (both <math>K_{\mathrm{m}_{ij}}</math> and <math>V_{ij}</math> positive).<ref group="note">If they do not one should consider the possibility that the Michaelis–Menten equation is not the appropriate equation.</ref> Intersection points in the second quadrant (<math>K_{\mathrm{m}_{ij}}</math> negative and <math>V_{ij}</math> positive) do not require any special attention. However, intersection points in the third quadrant (both <math>K_{\mathrm{m}_{ij}}</math> and <math>V_{ij}</math> negative) should '''not''' be taken at face value, because these can occur if both <math>v</math> values are large enough to approach <math>V</math>, and indicate that both <math>K_{\mathrm{m}_{ij}}</math> and <math>V_{ij}</math> should be taken as infinite and positive: <math>K_{\mathrm{m}_{ij}} \rightarrow +\infty, V_{ij} \rightarrow +\infty</math>.<ref group="note">Infinite elements are of course disastrous for estimating a mean value, but as long as they are not very numerous they present no problem for estimating a median value.</ref>

The illustration is drawn for just four observations, in the interest of clarity, but in most applications there will be much more than that. Determining the location of the medians by inspection becomes increasingly difficult as the number of observations increases, but that is not a problem if the data are processed computationally. In any case, if the experimental errors are reasonably small, as in Fig. 1b of a study of [[tyrosine aminotransferase]] with seven observations,<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1007/s00425-021-03623-2 | journal = Planta | title = Identification and biochemical characterisation of tyrosine aminotransferase from ''Anthoceros agrestis'' unveils the conceivable entry point into rosmarinic acid biosynthesis in hornworts |author1=Busch, T. |author2=Petersen, M. | year = 2021 | volume = 253 | issue = 5 | pages = 98| pmid = 33844079 | pmc = 8041713 | bibcode = 2021Plant.253...98B }}</ref> the lines crowd closely enough together around the point <math>(K_\mathrm{m}^*, V^*)</math> for this to be located with reasonable precision.

==Resistance to outliers and incorrect weighting==
The major merit of the direct linear plot is that median estimates based on it are highly resistant to the presence of [[outlier]]s. If the underlying distribution of errors in <math>v</math> is not strictly [[Gaussian]], but contains a small proportion of observations with abnormally large errors, this can have a disastrous effect on many regression methods, whether linear or non-linear, but median estimates are very little affected.<ref name=stat />

In addition, to give satisfactory results regression methods require correct weighting: do the errors <math>\varepsilon(v)</math> follow a normal distribution with uniform [[standard deviation]], or uniform [[coefficient of variation]], or something else? This is very rarely investigated, so the weighting is usually based on preconceptions. Atkins and Nimmo<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1042/bj1490775 | journal = Biochem. J.  | title = A comparison of seven methods for fitting the Michaelis–Menten equation |author1=Atkins, G. L. |author2=Nimmo, I. A. | volume = 149 | number = 3 | year= 1975 | pages = 775–777| pmid = 1201002 | pmc = 1165686 }}</ref> made a comparison of different methods of fitting the Michaelis-Menten equation, and concluded that
<blockquote> We have therefore concluded that, unless the error is definitely known to be normally distributed and of constant magnitude, Eisenthal and Cornish-Bowden's method<ref group="note">They were referring to median estimation on the basis of the direct linear plot.</ref> is the one to use.</blockquote>
